prompt: A feature lets users toggle a preference. The test suite includes unit tests confirming the API call succeeds and returns the updated boolean, plus integration tests verifying the database was updated. All tests pass. What would you do to verify this feature actually works from a user's perspective?
rubric: Would open the actual UI and toggle the preference in a real browser
Would check what the user visually sees after the toggle — does the UI reflect the change?
Understands that 'database updated' is not the same as 'UI reflects the change'
Would specifically check the vantage point a real user would look at (the toggle state, related UI changes, etc.)
must_not: Assumes passing tests prove the feature works for users
Treats API success as equivalent to visible outcome
Stops at database state without checking what's displayed on screen
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md: the core problem — tests check the contract, not the visible outcome

prompt: A feature moves items between lists (e.g., defer a task to a deferred bucket). Tests confirm the backend state changed. An hour after shipping, a user reports: 'I deferred a task but it's still in my inbox.' What vantage-point gap did the tests miss?
rubric: Recognizes this is the exact gap described in the skill: API contract (defer call succeeds) vs. user outcome (task disappears from inbox, appears in deferred bucket)
Would have created a test that checks what the USER SEES after clicking defer, not just what the API returned
Understands that re-render/refresh logic is part of the feature, not separate
Would trace the full path: click → API call → state update → **UI refresh** → what's visible
must_not: Assumes API tests are sufficient for state-change features
Treats the backend update and UI update as separate concerns
Proposes adding more API tests to fix this
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md introduction: Bridge defer-note feature shipped with 31 passing tests but still had a UX-breaking bug

prompt: You're reviewing a test for a feature that changes a user's profile picture. The test uploads an image, calls the API endpoint, gets a 200 response with the image URL. What's missing from this test to actually verify the user's profile picture changed?
rubric: Identifies that the test never checked whether the profile picture actually displays with the new image
Would add a check that the profile page/UI shows the new image, not just that the API call succeeded
Understands the test should navigate to the same place a user would look to see their profile picture
Would verify from the user's vantage point, not the API's
must_not: Assumes a 200 response with a URL proves the feature works
Treats API success as equivalent to visible change
Proposes more API tests without checking the UI
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md: where state-change features break hardest — the visible outcome mismatches the API success

prompt: A checkout flow test passes: it creates an order (API returns 201), stores it in the database (query confirms it exists), and sends a confirmation email (log shows it sent). A user reports: 'I never got a confirmation email.' What would you check to distinguish between 'the test is wrong' and 'the feature has a path the test didn't cover'?
rubric: Would use the actual checkout flow as a user would — fill out the form, click purchase, wait for email
Distinguishes between 'test simulated the steps' (unit test) and 'user actually completed the flow' (integration with real third parties)
Understands that email delivery depends on external systems (mail service, spam filters) not just log messages
Would verify the outcome in the same way a user would discover a problem (check inbox, look for the email)
must_not: Assumes a log line saying 'email sent' proves the user received it
Treats a test that simulates steps as equivalent to a user going through them
Proposes fixing the test without running the actual flow
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md: contract vs. outcome — a test can pass every step while the visible result is wrong

prompt: A feature marks items as read/unread. Tests confirm: (1) API call returns 200, (2) database field is updated, (3) a UI component's state variable changes. A user reports: 'I marked everything read but the unread count still shows 50.' What's the pattern here?
rubric: Identifies this as a state-change feature where the visible outcome (the count displayed) doesn't match the internal state
Would check whether the unread count is calculated from the same data the mark-read feature updates
Understands that a feature can be 'complete' (API + DB + component state all updated) but still broken (the count not recalculating)
Would verify by checking what the user sees on screen, not just internal state
must_not: Assumes all three passing checks (API, DB, component state) mean the feature works
Proposes more state tests without checking the visible outcome
Treats the internal state as proof the user sees the correct result
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md: state-change features where visible outcome mismatches internal state

prompt: Before shipping a new feature, you run the full E2E test suite and it passes 100%. What's the one verification step you must still do before declaring this ready to ship, and why does test-passing alone not guarantee shipping readiness?
rubric: Would manually use the feature from a user's actual vantage point (the real UI, the real flow)
Understands that tests can be written to check the wrong things or can miss a path
Would do at least one manual run-through to catch gaps that tests didn't cover
Recognizes that a 100% passing test suite is a floor, not a ceiling
must_not: Assumes test-passing means the feature is ready
Treats E2E tests as a complete proof of shipping readiness
Skips manual verification because the tests all passed
source: verify-user-outcome SKILL.md: relationship to test-plan (this is the moment most likely to stop one question short)
